claim: The majority of clinically used antibiotics continue to be based on chemical scaffolds derived from natural products made by microbes, namely actinomycete bacteria and filamentous fungi.
source: The majority of clinically used antibiotics continue to be based on chemical scaffolds derived from natural products (also known as specialized metabolites) made by microbes, namely actinomycete bacteria and filamentous fungi (Chevrette and Currie, 2019; Gholami-Shabani et al., 2019; Hutchings et al., 2019; Lyu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The spread of resistance among pathogens has led to a steep erosion in antibiotic efficacy.
source: However, the spread of resistance among pathogens has led to a steep, and well-documented, erosion in antibiotic efficacy (Colavecchio et al., 2017; Lekshmi et al., 2017; Richardson, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Leafcutter ants protect their fungal gardens from a pathogenic fungus (Escovopsis sp.) by associating with actinomycetes usually belonging to the genus Pseudonocardia.
source: These ants protect their fungal gardens from a pathogenic fungus (Escovopsis sp.) by associating with actinomycetes usually belonging to the genus Pseudonocardia, which produce a variety of antifungal molecules (e.g., dentigerumycin and gerumycins) that differentially inhibit the growth of the Escovopsis sp. (Currie et al., 2003; Li et al., 2018; Menegatti et al., 2021; Oh et al., 2009; Sit et al., 2015; Van Arnam et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Pseudonocardia associated with leafcutter ants produce antifungal molecules including dentigerumycin and gerumycins that differentially inhibit the growth of Escovopsis sp.
source: These ants protect their fungal gardens from a pathogenic fungus (Escovopsis sp.) by associating with actinomycetes usually belonging to the genus Pseudonocardia, which produce a variety of antifungal molecules (e.g., dentigerumycin and gerumycins) that differentially inhibit the growth of the Escovopsis sp. (Currie et al., 2003; Li et al., 2018; Menegatti et al., 2021; Oh et al., 2009; Sit et al., 2015; Van Arnam et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The southern pine beetle maintains Streptomyces sp. capable of inhibiting fungal pathogens.
source: Similarly, the gregarious southern pine beetle, which cultivates fungi to feed its larvae, maintains Streptomyces sp. capable of inhibiting fungal pathogens (Scott et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Beewolf wasps harbor Streptomyces philanthi in specialized antennal reservoirs.
source: Another archetypal insect/actinomycete system includes the solitary beewolf wasps, which harbor Streptomyces philanthi in specialized antennal reservoirs (Kaltenpoth et al., 2005; Kaltenpoth et al., 2010; Kaltenpoth et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Female beewolves inoculate their brood chambers with Streptomyces symbionts, which are ultimately incorporated into the cocoons of their pupating larvae.
source: Female beewolves inoculate their brood chambers with these symbionts, which are ultimately incorporated into the cocoons of their pupating larvae (Kaltenpoth et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Streptomyces associated with beewolves produce a suite of antifungal molecules including piericidins and derivatives, streptochlorins, and nigericin that protect the brood from opportunistic fungal pathogens.
source: These Streptomyces produce a suite of antifungal molecules (piericidins and derivatives, streptochlorins, and nigericin) that protect the brood from opportunistic fungal pathogens (Engl et al., 2018; Kroiss et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Analyses of the leafcutter ant and beewolf systems have shown the co-evolution of the insect hosts and actinomycete symbionts, suggesting that these relationships have remained durable over tens of millions of years.
source: Importantly, analyses of the leafcutter ant and beewolf systems have shown the co-evolution of the insect hosts and actinomycete symbionts, suggesting that these relationships, and the molecules involved, have remained durable over tens of millions of years (Kaltenpoth et al., 2014; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both leafcutter ants and beewolves have specialized structures for maintaining their actinomycete symbionts, which facilitate vertical transmission and high symbiont fidelity.
source: Both leafcutter ants and beewolves have specialized structures for maintaining their actinomycete symbionts, which facilitate vertical transmission and high symbiont fidelity (Kaltenpoth et al., 2005; Li et al., 2018; Stubbendieck et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: O. disjunctus does not appear to have mycangia or other specialized structures that harbor microbial symbionts.
source: Notably, O. disjunctus does not appear to have mycangia or other specialized structures that harbor microbial symbionts (Ulyshen, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A previous study on tropical passalid beetles found a diverse community of actinomycetes inhabiting the gut of both adults and larvae.
source: While O. disjunctus has not been investigated for the presence of actinomycetes and antimicrobials, a previous study on tropical passalid beetles found a diverse community of actinomycetes inhabiting the gut of both adults and larvae (Vargas-Asensio et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Frass is an important nutrient source in the O. disjunctus system for both adult and larval survival, and pupal chamber construction.
source: Frass is an abundant and easily sampled material in O. disjunctus galleries, and it is an important nutrient source in this system for both adult and larval survival, and pupal chamber construction (Biedermann, 2020; Mason and Odum, 1969; Schuster and Schuster, 1985; Valenzuela-González, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: 76.1% of actinomycete isolates from O. disjunctus galleries displayed activity against B. subtilis and/or C. albicans.
source: Specifically, 76.1% of the collection displayed activity against B. subtilis and/or C. albicans (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1B—Table S2), with 48.7% inhibiting both.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1D.

claim: 48.7% of actinomycete isolates from O. disjunctus galleries inhibited both B. subtilis and C. albicans.
source: Specifically, 76.1% of the collection displayed activity against B. subtilis and/or C. albicans (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1B—Table S2), with 48.7% inhibiting both.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Seven distinct compound families were detected in O. disjunctus frass, including actinomycins D and X2, angucyclinones STA-21 and rubiginone B2, cycloheximide, nactins (monactin, dinactin, trinactin, and tetranactin), polyene macrolides (filipin III, filipin IV, and fungichromin), polycyclic tetramate macrolactams (alteramides A and B), and piericidin A.
source: Specifically, we detected 15 compounds that were grouped into seven distinct compound families based on high structural similarities (i.e., when analogs were grouped): the actinomycins D and X2 (1, 2); the angucyclinones STA-21 and rubiginone B2 (3, 4); cycloheximide (5); the nactins monactin, dinactin, trinactin, and tetranactin (7–10); the polyene macrolides filipin III, filipin IV, and fungichromin (13–15); the polycyclic tetramate macrolactams (PTMs) alteramides A and B (16, 17); and piericidin A (24) (Figure 2A; Supplementary files 1C—Table S3, 1D—Table S4; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical analysis data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 2A.

claim: All compound families detected in O. disjunctus frass are known to be produced by actinomycetes and to have antimicrobial properties.
source: All of these families of compounds are known to be produced by actinomycetes and to have antimicrobial properties (Gao et al., 2014; Hollstein, 1974; K'ominek, 1975; Mevers et al., 2017; Moree et al., 2014; Oka et al., 1990; Olano et al., 2014; Ortega et al., 2019; Protasov et al., 2017; Shih et al., 2003; Song et al., 2005; Taniguchi et al., 2002; Urakawa et al., 1996; Zizka, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The average number of compound families detected per O. disjunctus gallery was approximately 2.3.
source: The average number of compound families detected per gallery was ~2.3, with only one gallery containing no detectable compounds, and four galleries containing four or five compound families (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 2B.

claim: Four families of compounds (actinomycins, angucyclinones, nactins, and cycloheximide) were detected in pupal chamber material collected from gallery 17-LA.
source: Four families of compounds were detected in the pupal chamber material collected from gallery 17-LA: actinomycins, angucyclinones, polyene macrolides, and nactins.
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Beauvericin was detected in nearly half of the O. disjunctus galleries.
source: Interestingly, we also detected beauvericin, a compound with known insecticidal activity (Wang and Xu, 2012), in nearly half of the galleries (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical analysis data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 2C.

claim: Beauvericin is known to be produced by fungal entomopathogens like Beauveria spp. and Fusarium spp.
source: Beauvericin is known to be produced by fungal entomopathogens like Beauveria spp. and Fusarium spp. (Hamill et al., 1969; Logrieco et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: 25 compounds representing 12 distinct antimicrobial families plus 1 siderophore compound were identified from actinomycete isolates from O. disjunctus galleries.
source: In total, we identified 25 compounds representing 12 distinct antimicrobial families plus 1 siderophore compound.
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 14 of the compounds identified from O. disjunctus actinomycete isolates have been previously described to be produced by microbes associated with other insects.
source: We note that 14 of the compounds we identified here have been previously described to be produced by microbes associated with other insects (Benndorf et al., 2018; Blodgett et al., 2010; Engl et al., 2018; Grubbs et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2018; Kroiss et al., 2010; Mevers et al., 2017; Ortega et al., 2019; Poulsen et al., 2011; Schoenian et al., 2011; Seipke et al., 2011; Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and referenced in Figure 3.

claim: Actinomycetes from distant O. disjunctus galleries often produced the same compounds in vitro.
source: In the course of characterizing the richness of compounds produced by frass isolates, we observed that actinomycetes from distant galleries often produced the same compounds in vitro (Supplementary file 1B—Table S2).
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Actinomycins and filipins were consistently co-produced by a specific clade with high genetic relatedness, identified as Streptomyces padanus, which was found in almost all galleries (19/22).
source: For example, actinomycins and filipins were consistently co-produced by a specific clade (bootstrap value of 100%) with high genetic relatedness, here identified as Streptomyces padanus, which was found in almost all galleries (19/22, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic and chemical analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Distinct clades with high sequence similarity produced angucyclinones and bafilomycins, identified as Streptomyces scopuliridis and Streptomyces cellostaticus, respectively.
source: We also noted that distinct clades with high sequence similarity produced angucyclinones and bafilomycins, identified as Streptomyces scopuliridis and Streptomyces cellostaticus, respectively (bootstrap values of 100%).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic and chemical analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The S. padanus, S. scopuliridis, and S. cellostaticus clades are composed of highly related strains despite being isolated from geographically distant galleries (as far as ~1900 km, 10 degrees of latitude, and 18 degrees of longitude apart).
source: These clades are each composed of highly related strains despite being isolated from geographically distant galleries (as far as ~1900 km, 10 degrees of latitude, and 18 degrees of longitude apart; see Figure 4—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic and geographic data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4 supplements.

claim: Representatives of all three stable clades (S. padanus, S. scopuliridis, and S. cellostaticus) were isolated from the fresh frass of adults and larvae.
source: Notably, representatives of all three stable clades were isolated from the fresh frass, which serves as a proxy for the gut content, of adults and larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by isolation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: S. scopuliridis was isolated from pupal chamber material.
source: S. scopuliridis was also isolated from pupal chamber material, which is composed of frass (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by isolation data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4.

claim: Streptomyces DNA is present along the adult O. disjunctus digestive tract and is enriched in the posterior hindgut.
source: Additionally, an analysis of metagenomic data previously generated by members of our team confirmed that Streptomyces DNA is present along the adult O. disjunctus digestive tract and is enriched in the posterior hindgut (Supplementary file 7), the region in which remaining woody biomass is packed for its release in the form of frass.
evidence: The claim is supported by metagenomic data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Actinomycin X2 displayed robust synergism with both filipins and the angucyclinone STA-21 against M. anisopliae P287.
source: Actinomycin X2 displayed robust synergism with both the filipins and the angucyclinone STA-21 (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5.

claim: Actinomycin X2 displayed an antagonistic effect when tested in combination with nactins against M. anisopliae P287.
source: In contrast, actinomycin X2 displayed an antagonistic effect when tested in combination with nactins (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5.

claim: The combination of filipins and STA-21 showed a strongly antagonistic effect against M. anisopliae P287.
source: The combination of filipins and STA-21 (Figure 5D) also showed a strongly antagonistic effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 5.

claim: All three Streptomyces strains (S. padanus P333, S. scopuliridis P239, and S. californicus P327) strongly inhibited M. anisopliae P016 and P287 growth in frass.
source: All three Streptomyces strains strongly inhibited M. anisopliae P016 and P287 growth in frass (p<0.001, Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6D.

claim: S. padanus P333 produced actinomycins and filipins while growing in frass.
source: Metabolomics analysis of crude extracts of the frass material revealed the presence of the actinomycins and filipins produced by S. padanus, nactins and alteramides produced by S. californicus, and angucyclinones produced by S. scopuliridis, matching the compounds produced in vitro by these three Streptomyces (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6F.

claim: S. californicus P327 produced nactins and alteramides while growing in frass.
source: Metabolomics analysis of crude extracts of the frass material revealed the presence of the actinomycins and filipins produced by S. padanus, nactins and alteramides produced by S. californicus, and angucyclinones produced by S. scopuliridis, matching the compounds produced in vitro by these three Streptomyces (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6F.

claim: S. scopuliridis P239 produced angucyclinones while growing in frass.
source: Metabolomics analysis of crude extracts of the frass material revealed the presence of the actinomycins and filipins produced by S. padanus, nactins and alteramides produced by S. californicus, and angucyclinones produced by S. scopuliridis, matching the compounds produced in vitro by these three Streptomyces (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6F.

claim: The growth of S. padanus P333 was not affected by either S. californicus P327 or S. scopuliridis when co-inoculated on frass.
source: When we co-inoculated pairs of streptomyces on frass, the growth of S. padanus P333 was not affected by either S. californicus P327 or S. scopuliridis (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6E.

claim: S. padanus P333 strongly inhibited the growth of S. californicus P327 when co-inoculated on frass.
source: However, S. padanus P333 strongly inhibited the growth of S. californicus P327.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Production of the angucyclinone STA-21 by S. scopuliridis P239 was dramatically reduced when co-inoculated with S. padanus P333 in frass.
source: However, we noted that production of the angucyclinone STA-21, which is produced by S. scopuliridis P239, was dramatically reduced when S. scopuliridis P239 and S. padanus P333 were co-inoculated in frass, suggesting that S. padanus likely had a negative impact on S. scopuliridis P239 in this treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6 supplement 3.

claim: O. disjunctus is subsocial, with mating pairs establishing galleries within decaying logs where they rear their larvae.
source: O. disjunctus is subsocial, with mating pairs establishing galleries within decaying logs where they rear their larvae (Schuster and Schuster, 1985; Wicknick and Miskelly, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: O. disjunctus is coprophagic, and it is thought that microbes within frass continue digesting plant material as a kind of 'external rumen' between periods of consumption by the beetles.
source: O. disjunctus is also coprophagic, and it is thought that microbes within frass continue digesting plant material as a kind of 'external rumen' between periods of consumption by the beetles (Biedermann, 2020; Mason and Odum, 1969; Ulyshen, 2018; Valenzuela-González, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: O. disjunctus adults feed frass to the larvae.
source: The frass is also notable as the adults feed it to the larvae, and parents and teneral siblings construct chambers from frass around metamorphosing pupa (Biedermann, 2020; Gray, 1946; Schuster and Schuster, 1985; Valenzuela-González, 1992; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and referenced in Figure 1C.

claim: O. disjunctus parents and teneral siblings construct chambers from frass around metamorphosing pupa.
source: The frass is also notable as the adults feed it to the larvae, and parents and teneral siblings construct chambers from frass around metamorphosing pupa (Biedermann, 2020; Gray, 1946; Schuster and Schuster, 1985; Valenzuela-González, 1992; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and referenced in Figure 1C.

claim: 22 O. disjunctus galleries were sampled across eastern North America.
source: To investigate if actinomycetes were associated with O. disjunctus galleries, we sampled material from 22 galleries across eastern North America (Figure 1E, Supplementary file 1A—Table S1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sampling data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 1E.

claim: 339 bacterial strains were isolated from O. disjunctus galleries using two selective media to enrich for actinomycetes.
source: Using two selective media to enrich for actinomycetes, we isolated 339 bacterial strains (Supplementary file 1B—Table S2) and assayed their ability to inhibit growth of the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis and the fungal pathogen Candida albicans.
evidence: The claim is supported by isolation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Four families of compounds (actinomycins, angucyclinones, nactins, and cycloheximide) were found throughout the range of O. disjunctus, with each compound being represented in colonies separated by >1900 km.
source: Remarkably, four of the seven actinomycete compound families we detected in situ, including actinomycins, angucyclinones, nactins, and cycloheximide, were found throughout the range of O. disjunctus, with each compound being represented in colonies separated by >1900 km.
evidence: The claim is supported by chemical analysis and geographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: S. padanus P333 and S. scopuliridis P239 were able to produce robust zones of inhibition against both M. anisopliae strains in a plate-based assay.
source: This assay showed that S. padanus P333 and S. scopuliridis P239 were able to produce robust zones of inhibition against both M. anisopliae strains, while S. californicus P327 did not (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6B.

claim: S. californicus P327 did not produce zones of inhibition against M. anisopliae strains in a plate-based assay.
source: This assay showed that S. padanus P333 and S. scopuliridis P239 were able to produce robust zones of inhibition against both M. anisopliae strains, while S. californicus P327 did not (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6B.

claim: All microorganisms tested (including M. anisopliae P016, M. anisopliae P287, S. padanus P333, S. californicus P327, and S. scopuliridis P239) were able to use frass as a substrate for growth.
source: All microorganisms were able to use frass as a substrate for growth, including both M. anisopliae strains whose growth was enhanced ~14–20-fold compared to the no frass control (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6C.

claim: M. anisopliae P016 and P287 growth was enhanced approximately 14-20-fold when grown in frass compared to the no frass control.
source: All microorganisms were able to use frass as a substrate for growth, including both M. anisopliae strains whose growth was enhanced ~14–20-fold compared to the no frass control (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 6C.

claim: The O. disjunctus/actinomycete system represents a tractable system for exploration of actinomycete specialized metabolism at multiple scales, ranging from macroscale biogeography in natura to interactions of microbes at microscopic scales in vitro.
source: Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the O. disjunctus/actinomycete system represents a tractable system for exploration of actinomycete specialized metabolism at multiple scales, ranging from macroscale biogeography in natura to interactions of microbes at microscopic scales in vitro.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The rich array of antimicrobials produced by actinomycetes in O. disjunctus frass likely aids in gallery hygiene and protects both an important nutrient source for O. disjunctus and their pupae.
source: These findings support a model in which the lifestyle of O. disjunctus accommodates multiple Streptomyces lineages in their frass, resulting in a rich repertoire of antimicrobials that likely insulates their galleries against pathogenic invasion.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Coprophagy could be a mode of transmission of Streptomyces in O. disjunctus since the larvae are thought to exclusively consume frass fed to them by adult beetles.
source: These findings support the notion that coprophagy could be a mode of transmission of these microbes since the larvae are thought to exclusively consume frass fed to them by adult beetles (Valenzuela-González, 1992).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the isolation data and cited literature.

claim: The O. disjunctus system appears capable of maintaining both stable members and migrants that are constantly sampled from the surrounding environment.
source: Based on this evidence, the O. disjunctus system appears capable of maintaining both stable members and migrants that are constantly sampled from the surrounding environment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the phylogenetic and chemical analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The relatively non-specific nature of coprophagy as a microbial transmission mechanism may enable multiple Streptomyces lineages to competitively inhabit the O. disjunctus system, resulting in a correspondingly wide profile of antimicrobials with varied mechanisms of action.
source: Thus, we suggest that in the case of O. disjunctus the relatively non-specific nature of coprophagy as a microbial transmission mechanism may enable multiple Streptomyces lineages to competitively inhabit this system, resulting in a correspondingly wide profile of antimicrobials with varied mechanisms of action.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Synergism may potentiate the antimicrobial activity of multiple molecules produced by single strains, as well as molecules produced across species in O. disjunctus frass.
source: Thus, synergism may potentiate the antimicrobial activity of multiple molecules produced by single strains, as well as molecules produced across species.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the synergism data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The actinomycete community in O. disjunctus frass likely produces an ever-shifting landscape of antimicrobial combinations, where their activities are constantly enhanced or dampened, but also buffered against the development of pathogen resistance.
source: Collectively, our in vitro results, and the distributions of antimicrobials we detected in situ, lead us to speculate that the actinomycete community in frass likely produces an ever-shifting landscape of antimicrobial combinations, where their activities are constantly enhanced or dampened, but also buffered against the development of pathogen resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the synergism/antagonism data and in situ detection of antimicrobials.

claim: The specialized metabolite richness observed in O. disjunctus frass surpasses that described for beewolves and leafcutter ants.
source: The specialized metabolite richness we observe directly in frass from wild O. disjunctus galleries surpasses that described for beewolves and leafcutter ants.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the findings in this manuscript with published literature on other insect/actinomycete systems.

claim: By partnering with insects, actinomycetes and their specialized metabolite arsenals can escape normally strong latitudinal constraints observed in soil-dwelling streptomycetes.
source: Thus, results presented here, combined with the studies of beewolf wasps/S. philanthi, suggest that by partnering with insects, actinomycetes and their specialized metabolite arsenals can escape normally strong latitudinal constraints.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the biogeographic data presented in the manuscript and comparison with published literature on soil-dwelling streptomycetes.

claim: Streptomyces species that are candidates for stable members within the O. disjunctus system (i.e., the S. padanus, S. scopuliridis, and S. cellostaticus clades) were found in galleries distributed across 10 degrees of latitude.
source: Notably, Streptomyces species that are candidates for stable members within this system (i.e., the S. padanus, S. scopuliridis, and S. cellostaticus clades) were found in galleries distributed across 10 degrees of latitude.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic and geographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Previous studies demonstrated that soil-dwelling streptomycetes, and specialized metabolite biosynthetic gene clusters in soil, were limited to much narrower latitudinal distributions than insect-associated streptomycetes.
source: Specifically, previous studies demonstrated that soil-dwelling streptomycetes, and specialized metabolite biosynthetic gene clusters in soil, were limited to much narrower latitudinal distributions (Charlop-Powers et al., 2015; Choudoir et al., 2016; Lemetre et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The frass itself is composed of partially digested wood with high organic carbon content, and nitrogen fixation by microbes in the gut of O. disjunctus enhances its bioavailable nitrogen content.
source: The frass itself is composed of partially digested wood with high organic carbon content, and nitrogen fixation by microbes in the gut of O. disjunctus enhances its bioavailable nitrogen content as well (Ceja-Navarro et al., 2014; Ceja-Navarro et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Only actinomycin X2 and piericidin A have previously been directly detected in material associated with insects.
source: Of these compounds, only actinomycin X2 and piericidin A have previously been directly detected in material associated with insects, for example, waste material of laboratory colonies of Acromyrmex echinatior (a species of Attine ant) and associated with beewolf antennal glands and cocoons, respectively (Engl et al., 2018; Kaltenpoth et al., 2016; Kroiss et al., 2010; Ortega et al., 2019; Schoenian et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: This work expands the list of antimicrobials detected directly in material associated with insects to include the PTMs, polyene macrolides, cycloheximide, nactins, and angucyclinones.
source: This work expands the list of antimicrobials detected directly in material associated with insects to include the PTMs, polyene macrolides, cycloheximide, nactins, and angucyclinones.
evidence: The claim is based on the chemical detection data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Subsocial insects, such as O. disjunctus, are at higher risk than solitary insects of pathogenic spread due to their frequent social interactions.
source: Moreover, subsocial insects, such as O. disjunctus, are at higher risk than solitary insects of pathogenic spread due to their frequent social interactions (Onchuru et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Streptomyces spp. are known producers of enzymes that degrade wood components, for example, cellulose, lignin, and xylose.
source: It is important to note that Streptomyces spp. are also known producers of enzymes that degrade wood components, for example, cellulose, lignin, and xylose (Book et al., 2014; Book et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The streptomycete community associated with O. disjunctus may play a nutritional role in this system.
source: Therefore, the streptomycete community associated with O. disjunctus may play a nutritional role in this system as well.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from known capabilities of Streptomyces and cited literature.

claim: Vargas-Asensio et al., 2014 provided strong evidence that Streptomyces play an important role as nutritional symbionts in tropical passalid beetles from Central America.
source: Indeed, Vargas-Asensio et al., 2014 provided strong evidence that Streptomyces play an important role as nutritional symbionts in tropical passalid beetles from Central America (Vargas-Asensio et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The beewolf system contains the highest level of symbiote specificity, with a single species (or species complex) of streptomycete symbiont, and a relatively low diversity of chemical scaffolds that vary in their relative concentrations.
source: The beewolf system contains the highest level of symbiote specificity, with a single species (or species complex) of streptomycete symbiont, and a relatively low diversity of chemical scaffolds that vary in their relative concentrations (Engl et al., 2018; Kaltenpoth et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Various species of leafcutter ants appear to have changed actinomycete partners multiple times throughout the history of their symbioses, which has likely led to increased diversity of associated antimicrobials found across and within species of leafcutter ants.
source: In contrast, various species of leafcutter ants appear to have changed actinomycete partners multiple times throughout the history of their symbioses (Cafaro et al., 2011; Li et al., 2018; McDonald et al., 2019), which has likely led to increased diversity of associated antimicrobials found across and within species of leafcutter ants.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and inference about the consequences of partner switching.

claim: The high nutritional content of frass and the important role it plays in O. disjunctus social interactions may place a premium on maximizing antimicrobial diversity in this material.
source: One possible explanation for this richness is that the unique vulnerabilities associated with the high nutritional content of frass, and the important role it plays in O. disjunctus social interactions, may place a premium on maximizing antimicrobial diversity in this material.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the selective pressures in the O. disjunctus system.

claim: Multiple types of opportunistic fungal pathogens, including M. anisopliae, and possibly Beauveria spp. and/or Fusarium spp., appear to be common residents in O. disjunctus galleries.
source: This may be especially advantageous given that multiple types of opportunistic fungal pathogens, including M. anisopliae (based on isolations), and possibly Beauveria spp. and/or Fusarium spp. (based on detection of beauvericin), appear to be common residents in O. disjunctus galleries.
evidence: The claim is based on isolation and chemical detection data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many O. disjunctus isolates were grouped in clades with a high representation of strains isolated from a wide range of insects from distant locations.
source: This tree showed that many O. disjunctus isolates were grouped in clades with a high representation of strains isolated from a wide range of insects from distant locations (Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis data presented in the manuscript and referenced in Figure 4 supplement 8.

claim: The 16S rRNA gene sequences of many of the Streptomyces isolated from O. disjunctus largely grouped with other insect-associated Streptomyces strains from around the world, indicating that they may be representatives of lineages that readily form stable relationships with insects.
source: Additionally, the 16S rRNA gene sequences of many of the Streptomyces we isolated from O. disjunctus largely grouped with other insect-associated Streptomyces strains from around the world, indicating that they may be representatives of lineages that readily form stable relationships with insects.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from phylogenetic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Antagonism between molecules can guard against the evolution of antimicrobial resistance.
source: While antagonism between molecules in frass may lead to diminished potency in the short term, emerging evidence indicates that antagonism can guard against the evolution of antimicrobial resistance (Chait et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: An environment with an ever-shifting landscape of antimicrobial combinations may present a more challenging target for would-be pathogens compared to one in which a single antimicrobial, or antimicrobial combination, is dominant.
source: We hypothesize that such an environment may present a more challenging target for would-be pathogens compared to one in which a single antimicrobial, or antimicrobial combination, is dominant.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the ecological consequences of antimicrobial diversity.

claim: The O. disjunctus/actinomycete system provides a new platform for investigation of the chemical ecology of specialized metabolites.
source: The O. disjunctus/actinomycete system provides a new platform for investigation of the chemical ecology of specialized metabolites.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The O. disjunctus lifestyle enables both microbial and chemical richness in their galleries.
source: In contrast to archetypal insect/actinomycete symbioses that rely on highly specific symbiotes that produce a limited number of antimicrobial compounds, our results suggest that the O. disjunctus lifestyle enables both microbial and chemical richness in their galleries.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Continued exploration of novel insect/actinomycete systems will be critical to gaining a complete understanding of the strategies and mechanisms that underpin evolutionarily durable chemical defenses against pathogenic microbes in natural settings.
source: Continued exploration of novel insect/actinomycete systems will be critical to gaining a complete understanding of the strategies and mechanisms that underpin evolutionarily durable chemical defenses against pathogenic microbes in natural settings.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' perspective on the implications of their findings.
